---
title: "Hand-wiring"
---

```{python}
#| label: setup-hand-wiring
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup: the demo's `Orders` schema, which every example on this page uses"
#| output: false
from collections.abc import Iterator

import dagster as dg
import dataframely as dy
import polars as pl

import dagster_dataframely as dd
from dagster_dataframely_demo.schema import Orders
from dagster_dataframely_demo._data import storefront_orders


def orders_frame() -> pl.LazyFrame:
    return storefront_orders().lazy()
```

Use `dd.asset` where you can.
One declaration fills the Columns tab, reports every rule as an asset check, filters the rows and, with `filter=True`, writes the error rows.
`dd.asset` calls functions that `dd.wiring` also exports.
Use them where `dd.asset` cannot build the asset: to attach a schema to an asset declared some other way, or to report checks in a way `dd.asset` does not offer.

Together, the functions do less than `dd.asset`: you pass them the settings and asset keys that `dd.asset` resolves at definition time.
This package will add nothing to `dd.wiring` to make reassembling the decorator easier.
To see how `dd.asset` calls the functions, read its source, which is short.

In the examples, `orders_frame()` represents whatever produces your frame.

## The parts

**The Columns tab.**
`get_column_schema_metadata(schema)` returns the definition metadata that an asset built with `dd.asset` declares.
Pass it as the `metadata` of any `@dg.asset`, and the Columns tab shows the schema: dtypes, descriptions, nullability, uniqueness, the primary key at table level, and every other column constraint next to its column.
It returns a mapping with one entry, so you can merge it with your own `metadata`.
`dd.asset` merges it last, so its entry takes precedence over any `dagster/column_schema` in yours.
`get_table_schema(schema)` returns the `dg.TableSchema` in that entry.
Put it under `dagster/column_schema` in a metadata dict you build yourself.

An IO manager can write its own column schema to the materialization: `PolarsParquetIOManager` writes one from the frame, with no constraints.
After a run under such an IO manager, the Columns tab takes the dtypes, nullability and constraints from that schema, and only the descriptions and tags from the definition.
Dagster merges an IO manager's metadata over a returned `dg.MaterializeResult`'s, and merges `add_asset_metadata` over both.
So in a run, `dd.asset` also calls `context.add_asset_metadata(get_column_schema_metadata(schema))`, and a hand-wired asset needs the same call to keep the full schema after a run.

Column tags come from `dy.Column(metadata=...)`, which Dataframely stores but does not use.
`get_table_schema` converts tag values to strings, because `dg.TableColumn.tags` is `Mapping[str, str]` and Dagster rejects any other type at definition time.

The Columns tab reads `unique` from each column's own flag, never from `primary_key`.
Dataframely checks a primary key with one schema-level rule and does not set the key columns' `unique` flag.
For a composite key, marking each column unique would show a constraint that no rule checks.

**The code version.**
`get_code_version(schema)` returns the code version that `dd.asset` sets when it gets none, as [The code version](declaring-an-asset.qmd#the-code-version) describes.
Pass it as the `code_version` of `@dg.asset`.

**The checks.**
`build_asset_check_specs(schema, asset=key)` returns a spec for every check the schema defines, including the column-schema check.
For a partitioned asset, also pass its `partitions_def`, so Dagster records each check evaluation under its partition.
Pass `filter=True` when the asset writes error rows, as `dd.asset(filter=True)` does, so that no rule's check is blocking.
`evaluate_checks(schema, frame, asset_key=key)` yields a result for each of those checks and writes nothing.
Each failing check has its rule's severity, as in `dd.asset`.
Pass the same `check_granularity` to `build_asset_check_specs` and to the function that yields the results, or to neither.
The setting determines the check names.
Dagster matches each result to its spec by name, so different values fail the step.

**Validation and the write.**
An asset built with `dd.asset` runs `stream_results(schema, frame, asset_key=key, error_rows_writer=...)` after its decorated function.
It runs the column-schema check and `Schema.filter`, writes the error rows, and yields the materialization and every check result.
Its return type is `Iterator[dg.MaterializeResult | dg.AssetCheckResult]`, which a hand-wired asset's function uses as its own annotation.
The writer writes the error rows, and `stream_results` yields no result for them.
For a partitioned asset, also pass `partitioned=True`, so the row count is under `dagster/partition_row_count` instead of `dagster/row_count`.
You make one choice that changes what a run writes: whether to pass `error_rows_writer`.
The data determines the rest.

<!-- rumdl-disable-next-line MD078 -->
```{mermaid}
%%| label: hand-wiring-runs
flowchart TD
    F["frame passed to stream_results"] --> N{"None?"}
    N -- yes --> SKIP["nothing written<br/>every check passes<br/>run succeeds"]
    N -- no --> CS{"column schema matches?"}
    CS -- no --> DRIFT["nothing written<br/>dy_schema__columns fails, ERROR<br/>rules never evaluated<br/>run fails, ColumnSchemaError"]
    CS -- yes --> FILTER["Schema.filter"]
    FILTER --> ANY{"a row failed an 'error' rule?"}
    ANY -- no --> CLEAN["every row written<br/>error rows written empty, if a writer was passed<br/>run succeeds"]
    ANY -- yes --> Q{"error_rows_writer passed?"}
    Q -- no --> ABORT["nothing written<br/>run fails, ValidationAbortError"]
    Q -- yes --> SURV{"any other rows?"}
    SURV -- no --> NONE["error rows written, table not written<br/>run fails, NoValidRowsError"]
    SURV -- yes --> PARTIAL["table and error rows written<br/>run succeeds"]
```

Every failing check has its rule's severity, in every kind of run.
[Validation](validation.qmd) and [Filtering error rows](filtering-error-rows.qmd) list the same five kinds of run as tables, with what each one writes.

**The error rows.**
`stream_results` takes an `ErrorRowsWriter`: a function that receives the rows that failed an `"error"` rule, writes them and returns the error-rows address.
The address is a string, not a path, because it can name a database table.
When no row fails an `"error"` rule, the writer receives a frame with zero rows and the same columns, so a writer that overwrites replaces the last run's error rows.

In a run, `dd.asset` uses `build_io_manager_writer(context)`.
It passes the rows to the asset's own IO manager, under the asset key `<name>__error_rows`.
That IO manager writes them as it writes any asset with that key.
The IO manager receives a copy of the step's output context with only the asset key changed, so a database IO manager still reads its connection settings from it.
`build_io_manager_writer` takes `error_rows_key=` and `error_rows_io_manager_key=`, which mean what they mean on `dd.asset`.
With `error_rows_io_manager_key=`, list the key in your asset's `required_resource_keys`.
After the write, the writer logs a materialization for the error-rows key with the metadata the IO manager added, as [Filtering error rows](filtering-error-rows.qmd) describes.
That metadata does not appear in the table's materialization, so the package reports the error-rows address itself.

`build_file_writer(key, error_rows_dir, partition_key)` is for direct invocation, which has no step and so no IO manager.
It writes only parquet.

`validate_error_rows_key(context)` fails the run with `ErrorRowsKeyCollisionError` when another asset in the code location already materializes `<name>__error_rows`.

`build_file_writer`, `validate_error_rows_key` and `get_error_rows_path` also take `error_rows_key=`.
Pass each one the same value, so the writer, the check and the path use the same key.

`build_error_rows_spec(schema, definition)` reads the error-rows key and the IO manager key from two metadata entries that only `dd.asset` writes.
So for a hand-wired asset that passes either keyword, set both on the spec yourself, with Dagster's own methods: `build_error_rows_spec(schema, orders).replace_attributes(key=...).with_io_manager_key(...)`.

`dd.wiring` also exports two lower-level functions.
`get_error_rows(schema, failure)` returns the frame every writer receives: the rows that failed an `"error"` rule, then one `String` rule column per rule, named in the reserved namespace.
Use it in an asset that runs `Schema.filter` itself, to write the same frame `dd.asset` would.
`get_error_rows_path(key, error_rows_dir, partition_key)` returns the path `build_file_writer` writes to, so a test can check the path without writing a file.

## The decorator is a `@dg.asset`, a writer and `stream_results`

Pass the schema's metadata and check specs to `@dg.asset`, and call `stream_results` in the body:

```{python}
#| label: hand-wiring-1
@dg.asset(
    metadata=dd.wiring.get_column_schema_metadata(Orders),
    check_specs=dd.wiring.build_asset_check_specs(Orders, asset="orders", filter=True),
    code_version=dd.wiring.get_code_version(Orders),
    output_required=False,
)
def orders(
    context: dg.AssetExecutionContext,
) -> Iterator[dg.MaterializeResult | dg.AssetCheckResult]:
    dd.wiring.validate_error_rows_key(context)
    context.add_asset_metadata(dd.wiring.get_column_schema_metadata(Orders))
    yield from dd.wiring.stream_results(
        Orders,
        orders_frame(),
        asset_key=context.asset_key,
        error_rows_writer=dd.wiring.build_io_manager_writer(context),
    )
```

This gives the asset the Columns tab, one check per rule, the code version, the row filter and the error rows.
For a single-output asset, `context.asset_key` is the only key you need.

When the frame matches the schema, a run of that asset makes these calls:

<!-- rumdl-disable-next-line MD078 -->
```{mermaid}
%%| label: hand-wiring-sequence
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as orders
    participant V as stream_results
    participant W as build_io_manager_writer
    participant D as Dagster
    A->>V: Orders, frame, asset_key, error_rows_writer
    V->>V: column-schema check
    V->>V: Schema.filter
    opt a writer was passed
        V->>W: error rows
        W-->>D: the error rows' AssetMaterialization
        W-->>V: error-rows address
    end
    opt the table was written
        V-->>D: MaterializeResult
    end
    V-->>D: an AssetCheckResult per check
```

`orders` passes the frame and the writer to `stream_results`.
`stream_results` calls the writer with the error rows, which have zero rows when no row failed an `"error"` rule.
The writer logs the error rows' materialization unless the code location has no spec for them.
It then returns the error-rows address.
`stream_results` then yields the `MaterializeResult` if it wrote the asset's table, and one result for each check.
`orders` passes each one to Dagster with `yield from`.

`output_required=False` lets the step end without yielding the materialization, which happens on a column-schema mismatch, on `ValidationAbortError`, on `NoValidRowsError` and on the skip.
Without it, every path that does not raise has to yield the output.

Without an `error_rows_writer`, a row that fails an `"error"` rule fails the run with `ValidationAbortError`, as in an asset built with `dd.asset` and `filter=False`.

`build_io_manager_writer` needs a step, so it raises `dagster._core.errors.DagsterInvalidPropertyError` under direct invocation.
There, `dd.asset` uses `build_file_writer(context.asset_key, error_rows_dir, partition_key)`, and you can do the same.
`context.add_asset_metadata` also fails under direct invocation, with `AttributeError`.
`dd.asset` makes the call only when `dg.AssetExecutionContext.get()` returns a context, which happens only in a run.

Call `validate_error_rows_key(context)` before the rest of the body, as `dd.asset` does on every run.
Under direct invocation it does nothing, because there is no asset graph to check.

## Split the checks off entirely

`dd.build_rule_checks` builds the checks for a table the IO manager has already written, as [Rule checks](rule-checks.qmd) shows.

## Without the package at all

Every example above uses `dd.wiring`.
This is the same asset without this package: the Columns tab, one check per rule, the column-schema check, the row filter and the error rows, all written by hand.

```{python}
#| label: hand-wiring-3
VALID = dg.AssetKey(["orders"])
ERROR_ROWS = dg.AssetKey(["orders__error_rows"])
COLUMNS = Orders.columns()
# Private in Dataframely: nothing public lists a schema's rules before it runs.
RULES = list(Orders._validation_rules(with_cast=False))


def get_check_name_for_rule(rule: str) -> str:
    return f"dy_rule__{rule.replace('|', '__')}"


COLUMN_SCHEMA = dg.TableSchema(
    columns=[
        dg.TableColumn(
            name=name,
            type=str(column.dtype),
            description=column.description,
            constraints=dg.TableColumnConstraints(
                nullable=column.nullable, unique=column.unique
            ),
        )
        for name, column in COLUMNS.items()
    ]
)


@dg.multi_asset(
    outs={
        "orders": dg.AssetOut(
            metadata={"dagster/column_schema": COLUMN_SCHEMA}, is_required=False
        ),
        "orders__error_rows": dg.AssetOut(is_required=False),
    },
    check_specs=[
        dg.AssetCheckSpec(name="dy_schema__columns", asset=VALID, blocking=True),
        *(
            dg.AssetCheckSpec(name=get_check_name_for_rule(rule), asset=VALID)
            for rule in RULES
        ),
    ],
)
def orders():
    # Eager, because `Schema.filter` returns a `LazyFrame` for a lazy frame and every
    # count below is a `len()`. The decorator does this collect for you.
    frame = orders_frame().collect()

    drift = {
        name: (column.dtype, frame.schema.get(name))
        for name, column in COLUMNS.items()
        if frame.schema.get(name) != column.dtype
    }
    yield dg.AssetCheckResult(
        check_name="dy_schema__columns", asset_key=VALID, passed=not drift
    )
    if drift:
        raise ValueError(f"{Orders.__name__} does not match the frame: {drift}")

    valid, failure = Orders.filter(frame, cast=False)
    counts = failure.counts()
    aborting = bool(len(failure)) and not len(valid)

    if len(valid):
        yield dg.MaterializeResult(
            asset_key=VALID, value=valid, metadata={"dagster/row_count": len(valid)}
        )
    if len(failure):
        rule_columns = {rule: get_check_name_for_rule(rule) for rule in RULES}
        invalid = failure.details().rename(rule_columns)
        yield dg.MaterializeResult(
            asset_key=ERROR_ROWS,
            value=invalid.with_columns(
                pl.col(name).cast(pl.String) for name in rule_columns.values()
            ),
            metadata={"dagster/row_count": len(failure)},
        )
    for rule in RULES:
        yield dg.AssetCheckResult(
            check_name=get_check_name_for_rule(rule),
            asset_key=VALID,
            passed=not counts.get(rule),
            severity=dg.AssetCheckSeverity.ERROR
            if aborting
            else dg.AssetCheckSeverity.WARN,
        )
```

That runs, and a run where some rows pass and some fail writes both tables.
It differs from `dd.asset` in these ways:

- It calls `Orders._validation_rules`, which is private.
  Dataframely has no public way to list a schema's rules before validation, so every check name and rule column here depends on an API with no deprecation guarantee.
  This package calls the same private API, and a characterization test checks it.
  So a change in Dataframely fails one of this package's tests, not your assets.
- The Columns tab shows dtypes, descriptions, nullability and uniqueness.
  The rest of what `Orders` declares is missing: no `>= 0`, no regex, no length bound, no table-level primary key, no column tags.
  After a run under an IO manager that writes its own column schema, the tab shows only that schema's dtypes and the descriptions.
- The checks have no descriptions, so a failing check shows the rule's name but not what the rule checks.
- No code version, so Dagster does not mark the asset stale after a schema edit.
- No statistics, no row sample, no failure examples and no `error_rows_by_rules` table, so a failing check shows nothing about the rows that failed it.
- No `check_granularity`, so a 40-column schema has around 40 checks or more, and you cannot collapse its rules into fewer checks.
- You have to collect and filter a `LazyFrame` yourself.
- No rule can be `"warn"`, and every failing check has the same severity, set by how the run ended.
- It has three kinds of run.
  A run where every row failed succeeds and skips the asset's table.
  `dd.asset` fails that run with `NoValidRowsError`, because `filter=True` lets a run succeed when some rows fail an `"error"` rule, not when every row does.
- It writes the error rows only when a row fails.
  So a clean run leaves the error rows from the last run that had any.
  `dd.asset` writes a frame with zero rows, so an IO manager that overwrites replaces them.
- The error rows are a second output of a `dg.multi_asset`, so the definition has two asset keys.
  `orders.key` raises `CheckError`.
  `@dg.asset(deps=[orders])` depends on the table and on the error rows.
  Inside the function, `context.asset_key` raises, and so does `context.add_asset_metadata` without `asset_key=`.
  A job that selects only `orders` raises `DagsterInvalidDefinitionError` when Dagster loads it.
- Nothing checks the names.
  A column already named `dy_rule__amount__min`, or two rules that produce the same check name, cause a silent collision instead of an error at definition time.
- With a `key_prefix`, you build both asset keys yourself, and nothing checks them.

### Or you could just do

```{python}
#| label: hand-wiring-4
@dd.asset(Orders, filter=True)
def orders(raw_orders: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    return raw_orders
```
